blocks.md: Cross-validation tests how well a model predicts data it has not seen. You hide part of the data, fit the model on the rest, and check how well it predicts the hidden part; then you rotate which part is hidden until every observation has been predicted once, and average the errors. A model that merely memorises its training data will look great in sample and poor here, so cross-validation exposes overfitting.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is the standard way to choose between models for prediction — for example, how many polynomial terms to include — when in-sample fit always favours the most complicated one.
A test of how well the model **generalises to new data**.

sections.heading: The holdout method and its problem

blocks.md: Split once into training (estimate parameters) and test (predict) sets. The estimate then depends on an arbitrary split.
Partition the data into $k$ mutually exclusive random folds, fit on $k-1$, predict the held-out fold, average over all $k$.

The lecture's crime example regresses crimes per person on population density in 630 observations. Holding out 25% gives a training RMSE of 0.01305 and a test RMSE of 0.01300; 5-fold CV gives fold RMSEs of 0.0086, 0.0147, 0.0108, 0.0185 and 0.0117, averaging 0.0129. The test error is no larger than the training error because a two-parameter line has little room to overfit; the spread across folds shows how much one holdout split can mislead.

blocks.md: Refitting wage on education on each set of four folds gives five nearly identical lines, another sign of a stable model (CV RMSE 11.66 dollars an hour).

blocks.md: The same exercise on the 50 cars moves the line more from fold to fold: with a small sample each held-out fifth matters (CV RMSE 14.97 feet).
Estimating **out-of-sample predictive error** and guarding against overfitting.

The lecture's application: fit polynomials of degree 1 to 5 in stopping distance to predict speed (the `cars` data, 50 cars) and pick the degree with the lowest CV error. In-sample error can only fall as the degree rises, so it would always pick degree 5; CV picks degree 1.

blocks.title: Correction to the lecture notebook
blocks.md: The notebook's cell builds the polynomial terms from `speed` and then predicts `speed`, so degrees 1 to 3 fit perfectly and its plot shows a CV RMSE of 0 that rises only at degrees 4 and 5. The table recomputes the intended model, speed on powers of stopping distance, with the same unshuffled 5-fold split. The conclusion survives: a low degree generalizes best and higher degrees overfit.

| Small $k$                                   | Large $k$ (up to leave-one-out, $k=n$) |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| More bias — each model trained on less data | Lower bias                             |
| Lower variance                              | Higher variance                        |
| Cheaper                                     | Expensive                              |

blocks.title: Important
blocks.md: **CV resamples to assess prediction. [Bootstrapping OLS](note:bootstrapping-ols) resamples to assess estimator uncertainty.** Different questions, same mechanical idea.
The bootstrap **cannot** detect overfitting, because every resample is drawn from the same data the model was fitted on — there is no held-out information.
